title: Research Interests
text: I am interested in how the brain builds reliable representations of the world during development, and in particular in the part that the cortex’s own internal structure plays in this process.

title: Research Interests
section: How the cortex prepares for seeing before it sees
text:
How the cortex prepares for seeing before it sees
Before eye opening, the visual cortex already shows richly structured spontaneous activity. I want to understand what this endogenous structure is good for: how it is shaped by recurrent connectivity, and how far it constrains what the cortex can later learn from experience.

title: Research Interests
section: How experience turns variable responses into reliable ones
text:
How experience turns variable responses into reliable ones
At eye opening, responses to the same stimulus differ from trial to trial; within days they become reliable. I am interested in the circuit mechanisms behind this transition. Our work so far suggests that reliability emerges when visual input becomes aligned with the pre-existing network structure, rather than through a general reduction of noise. See Trägenap et al., Nature Neuroscience 2025 (press release · free-to-read version).

title: Research Interests
text:
Feedforward input meets recurrent circuits
How do feedforward inputs and recurrent cortical circuits shape each other as the cortex matures? With the Fitzpatrick lab we found that coherent cortical responses develop as feedforward inputs become more discriminable and better aligned with the recurrent network. See Lempel, Trägenap et al., Neuron 2025 (press release · doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2025.08.014).

title: Research Interests
section: Selective amplification across the cortical sheet
text:
Selective amplification across the cortical sheet
Which activity patterns does the developing cortex amplify, and which does it suppress? With the Smith lab we study selective amplification on the scale of millimetres and ask which recurrent subnetworks can account for it. See Mulholland, Trägenap et al., bioRxiv 2026 (co-first authors; doi:10.64898/2026.03.31.715687).

title: Research Interests
section: Looking ahead: across the animal tree
text:
Looking ahead: across the animal tree
Most of what we know about cortical development comes from a handful of species. I would like to understand which developmental principles are general and which are specific to a particular brain. Comparing cortical organisation across species with different evolutionary histories and visual lifestyles, for example ferrets, cats, tree shrews and mice, is a way to find out. Where a species deviates from the others, the deviation itself becomes informative about the underlying mechanism.

title: Research Interests
section: Looking ahead: from biology to learning machines
text:
Looking ahead: from biology to learning machines
The developing cortex solves a problem that artificial systems also face: how to learn quickly from limited experience. I am curious whether the strategy we see in the brain, starting from a structured prior and aligning input to it, could make learning in artificial neural networks faster or more robust.

title: Research Interests
text:
Approach
I work at the interface of theory and experiment: dynamical recurrent network models, analysis of large-scale calcium imaging data, and the comparison of model predictions with chronically recorded neural populations. The data come from long-standing collaborations with the labs of David Fitzpatrick (Max Planck Florida Institute for Neuroscience) and Gordon Smith (University of Minnesota).

title: Outreach
text: I enjoy explaining how the brain learns to see to audiences outside the lab, most often in science slams: short, entertaining talks for a general audience. These talks are in German.

title: Outreach
text:
Interactive exhibit: EEG Mindball
Together with Bettina Hein, a former PhD student in our lab, I developed an EEG Mindball: an interactive exhibit in which visitors try to move a ball by producing a particular signal in their recorded EEG. It is modelled on an exhibit at the phaeno science centre in Wolfsburg and offers a hands-on introduction to brain signals. It has been shown at various events, such as the Hessen schafft Wissen exhibitions (for example at the Frankfurt Book Fair), the FIAS 20th anniversary, the Night of Science, and the FIAS booth at Frankfurt hat Hirn 2024.

title: Sigrid Trägenap
text:
I am a computational neuroscientist at the Frankfurt Institute for Advanced Studies (FIAS) and Goethe University Frankfurt, in the group of Matthias Kaschube.
I study how the developing visual cortex arrives at reliable representations of the world, combining recurrent network models with chronic imaging data from ferret visual cortex. I submitted my PhD thesis in January 2026.
